prompt: For disjoint cold arrays of 100 million float32 values, an AVX2 array-add compute kernel is only 1.1× faster than the scalar version. Measurements show both runs nearly saturate sustained DRAM bandwidth and neither has a substantial frequency drop. What best explains the small gain?

options.text: Memory bandwidth limits the loop: each element requires two input loads and an output store, potentially plus write-allocation traffic
options.explanation: Correct under the measured conditions. Faster arithmetic cannot remove the saturated traffic requirement.

options.text: AVX2 has no instruction for float addition
options.explanation: `vaddps` on `ymm` registers is AVX (and available with AVX2); float addition is fully supported.

options.text: The CPU must be downclocking heavily under AVX2
options.explanation: The stated measurements rule out a substantial clock reduction in these runs; no universal downclock limit is assumed.
There is no universal eightfold penalty; alignment and boundary-crossing costs are target-dependent.

workedExample:
Count bytes, then divide by bandwidth:

```formula
D = 10^8 × 16 B = 1.6 × 10^9 B
t_min = D / R
t_min = (1.6 × 10^9 B) /
        (50 × 10^9 B/s)
t_min = 0.032 s = 32 ms
P_max = (10^8 FLOP) / (0.032 s)
P_max ≈ 3.125 × 10^9 FLOP/s
where
D: total DRAM traffic, in bytes (B): 100 million elements × 16 bytes each (4 + 4 read, 4 read-for-ownership, 4 written back)
t_min: the shortest possible run time at full bandwidth, in seconds (s)
R: the sustained bandwidth; a hypothetical 50 GB/s = 50 × 10^9 B/s
P_max: the highest useful addition rate this traffic allows
B: byte
s: second
ms: millisecond, 0.001 s
FLOP: one floating-point operation (one addition here)
≈: approximately equal to
In words: moving 1.6 GB at 50 GB/s takes at least 32 ms whatever the arithmetic does, which caps the loop at about 3 billion additions a second.
```

Useful traffic is only 12 bytes per element; the extra 4 is the write-allocate read. This is a traffic bound, not proof that an arbitrary scalar loop reaches it; the prompt supplies the bandwidth measurements. Non-temporal stores or existing cached output can change the model.

prompt: Your library is built with `-march=haswell` (AVX2). Some customers on older servers report crashes with `SIGILL` (illegal instruction). What is the standard fix that keeps AVX2 speed where it is available?

options.explanation: The instruction will fault again every time: the CPU simply does not implement it.

options.text: Build for a baseline such as x86-64 (SSE2) and add runtime dispatch, so hot functions are also compiled for AVX2 and selected after checking all required CPU and OS register-state features
options.explanation: Correct. A supported multiversioning or dispatch mechanism can select a compatible compute kernel while the rest of the binary retains its baseline requirements.
That targets the build host rather than the supported deployment baseline, so compatibility still depends on the two machines.

options.text: Switch to AVX-512, which is backwards compatible
options.explanation: Older CPUs lacking AVX2 lack AVX-512 too; this would fail on even more machines.

workedExample: Compile baseline code for the oldest supported environment and specialised compute kernels separately. Dispatch only after checking every required extension and OS-enabled register state; AVX requires more than its CPUID feature bit. Test both fallback and accelerated paths. Feature-level names and -march targets may include instructions beyond AVX2 alone.
